study.title: Daniel 5 The profane banquet, the divine judgment, and the fall of Babylon
study.overview: Daniel 5 shows the contrast between human arrogance and the sovereignty of God. Belssazar irreverently uses the temple vessels, honors lifeless idols and, at the height of the feast, receives a mysterious writing that reveals that his kingdom has been counted, weighed and divided. Daniel interprets the message without accepting rewards, reminding the king that his guilt was not of ignorance, but of pride and conscious profanity. The chapter ends with the execution of the sentence: Belssazar dies that same night and Darius, fear, takes the kingdom. The text emphasizes that human kingdoms pass away, but the Most High God rules over them.

outline.title: The Feast of Belszzar and the desecration of the sacred vessels
outline.explanation: The chapter opens with a royal feast marked by excess, ostentation and irreverence. Belshazzar sends to bring the vessels taken from the temple of Jerusalem, and the use of these holy objects to drink wine and exalt idols reveals contempt for the God of Israel. Sin is not only idolatry in general, but the deliberate humiliation of what belonged to the worship of the Lord.

outline.title: The writing on the wall and the inability of the sages
outline.explanation: At the height of the party comes a hand writing on the wall, and the king is taken for extreme fear. The wise men of Babylon fail to read and explain the inscription, showing the limit of human wisdom before a direct act of divine judgment. Queen mother then remembers Daniel as someone endowed with light, intelligence, and ability to interpret puzzles.

outline.title: Daniel denounces pride and interprets the sentence
outline.explanation: Called to the presence of the king, Daniel refuses the gifts before speaking. He recalls Nebuchadnezzar's humiliation to show that Belsatis sinned with full knowledge: he exalted himself against the Lord, defiled the vessels of the temple, and praised gods that they do not see or hear. The inscription is deciphered as a sentence of counting, evaluation and division of the kingdom.

outline.title: The Empty Honor and Immediate Fall of Babylon
outline.explanation: Belsszar fulfills the protocol and honor Daniel, but this does not revoke the divine decree. That night the king is dead, and the kingdom passes to Darius, fear. The closure is dry and solemn: the judgment announced by God is fulfilled without delay.

study.context: The chapter takes place at the end of Babylonian dominion, when the city is about to fall before a new power. The notes indicate that Belshazzar ruled in Babylon as another Persian sovereign advanced; the chapter records the transition of empire as fulfillment of God's judgment on Babylon's pride. It is also relevant that the vessels of the temple of Jerusalem had been taken into exile and, according to the notes, would later be returned.
study.theology: The central theology of the chapter is God's absolute sovereignty over kings and empires. Belshazzar imagines that the political power and the luxury of the banquet guarantee security, but Daniel states that it was the Most High God who gave dominion to Nebuchadnezzar and who can withdraw kingdoms when he wants. The text also teaches that sin with knowledge increases guilt: Belshazzar was not only idolatrous, but despiseed the received light, profaned the saint and did not glorify the God who sustains his life and his ways. Writing on the wall works as a moral judgment: God weighs acts, not appearances; tells days, not discourses; and can close a dynasty in one night. There is also a contrast between true wisdom and empty wisdom: the court experts fail, while the servant of God correctly interprets reality.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter teaches that the earthly kingdoms pass through; the judgment of God came quickly that night and another kingdom took the place of Babylon.
Belsszar confronted God at the height of security, and the fall came just when his heart was joyful with wine.
The sacred vessels were profaned, and the text highlights Belshazzar's irreverence by using what belonged to the temple of the Lord.

questions: What attitudes today show the same contempt of Belszar for what is holy, even without explicit religious language?
In what areas can you be relying on apparent security while God is already evaluating your faithfulness?
How does the remembrance that God weighs kingdoms and hearts changes the way you use power, resources, and influence?
study.practice: This chapter calls concrete reverence. Avoid treating sacred things like display, convenience or vanity instruments. Examine whether there are areas in which you have received light on the right, but keep resisting to obey. Practice humility by remembering that positions, resources and reputation are not absolute; they are under the hand of God. It is also worth learning from Daniel: when called to speak, he does not negotiate the truth to gain personal advantage, but points the king to moral reality before the Lord.
study.uncertainty: The notes suggest different historical identities for Darius, fear, and also show uncertainty about the relationship between Belssazar and Nebuchadnezzar in the use of the word "father." Since the text provided does not clarify these questions in detail, this study treats this information as hypotheses mentioned by the commentators, not as indisputable certainties. It is also not possible, based only on the grades, to definitely solve the exact chronology proposed by each commentator.
